{{confused|urban bias}}
A '''metropolitan bias''' is a prejudice in favor of concentrated [[Urban area|urban]] population centers over more diffuse [[rural]] or [[suburban]] population areas. This is  described most often as a type of [[media bias]] in coverage of topics, as a general form of favoritism, or as a criticism raised in data gathering such as [[statistical study|statistical studies]] and [[Opinion poll|polling]].

==In media==
Television programs, especially news, have been criticized for covering urban centers disproportionately.<ref name="Oxford" />

In the [[United Kingdom]], the [[BBC]] was perceived to have a [[bias]] towards the [[London]] [[metropolitan area]], prompting [[ITV (TV network)|ITV]] to launch in the 1950s as a series of independent regional companies.<ref name="Oxford">{{cite book|last1=Chandler|first1=Daniel|last2=Munday|first2=Rod|title=A Dictionary of Media and Communication|date=2016|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|isbn=9780191057557|edition=2nd|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JFExDwAAQBAJ|via=[[Google Books]]|accessdate=10 May 2018|chapter=metropolitan bias|doi=10.1093/acref/9780199568758.001.0001}}</ref>

In 2007, BBC's coverage bias toward London was criticized by Scottish First Minister [[Alex Salmond]] ([[Scottish National Party|SNP]]) as "hideously [[White City, London|White City]]",<ref>{{cite book|last1=McGarvey|first1=Neil|title=Scottish Politics: An Introduction|date=2017|publisher=[[Palgrave Macmillan]]|isbn=9781137227560|page=41|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yplMDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA41|via=[[Google Books]]|accessdate=10 May 2018}}</ref> and Welsh [[Member of Parliament|MP]] [[Adam Price]] ([[Plaid Cymru]]) threatened to withhold part of the [[Television licensing in the United Kingdom|license fee]] over "minuscule" [[Wales]] coverage.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/wales/6955263.stm |title=Plaid MP's BBC licence fee threat|publisher=BBC News|work=[[BBC News Online]]|date=20 August 2007|access-date=10 May 2018}}</ref>

The BBC corporation's governance body, [[BBC Trust]], produced a 2014 report indicating bias against coverage related to rural England, though noting Wales and Scotland coverage was more balanced.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Spence|first1=Alex|title=BBC accused of an urban bias in its news coverage|via=[[Academic OneFile]]|work=[[The Times]]|date=June 17, 2014|location=London, England|page=10|quote=A BBC Trust report will say that the public broadcaster's news and current affairs programmes too often fail to reflect the wide range of interests outside of England's main urban centres. "One of the main points in the report is that the BBC does not seem to respect the experience of the wider population of England," an insider who has seen the report said. "In Wales and Scotland the BBC's current affairs is much more satisfactory. It's in England where the metropolitan bias starts to creep in."}}</ref>

==In resource allocation==
The term 'metropolitan bias' has been used to describe unequal [[resource allocation|allocation of resources]], such as governmental services.<ref name="Ferré" />

In one study, Ferré et al (2010) noted that, in the 1970s to 1980s, "[[urban bias]]" was a tendency of governments to disproportionately tax rural activities like agriculture and invest in urban-based industrialization. By 2010, they state, 75% of those living in [[extreme poverty]] (defined as less than $1 per day) lived in rural settings. In eight developing countries examined ([[Albania]], [[Brazil]], [[Kazakhstan]], [[Kenya]], [[Mexico]], [[Morocco]], [[Thailand]], and [[Sri Lanka]]), the authors noted a disproportional amount of services for the poor were available in urban areas. They concluded that "any strategy for urban poverty reduction that places greater focus on, or allocates more resources to, metropolitan areas, suffers from a 'metropolitan bias' analogous to the urban bias of old."<ref name="Ferré">{{cite journal|last1=Ferré|first1=Céline|last2=Ferreira|first2=Francisco H.G.|last3=Lanjouw|first3=Peter|title=Is there a metropolitan bias? The inverse relationship between poverty and city size in selected developing countries|publisher=[[World Bank]]|date=December 1, 2010|issue=Policy Research Working Paper No. 5508|ssrn=1732387}}</ref>

==In other areas==
In 2000, several [[architect]]s from [[Scotland]] and [[Wales]] made claims of metropolitan bias in selections for the [[Stirling Prize]] after five out of seven designs [[shortlist]]ed by judges were located within [[London]], despite the scope of the contest at the time extending to all of Europe. Critics also described the list as "London-centric". The chairman representing the judges in the contest dismissed the claims, noting that the first Stirling Prize was awarded to a building in [[Manchester]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Alberge|first1=Dalya|title=Prize case of London bias, say architects|work=[[The Times]]|date=4 Nov 2000|location=London, England|page=9|via=Academic OneFile|quote=Architects in Scotland and Wales have accused the judges of the Stirling Prize, the architecture world's answer to the Turner Prize, of "metropolitan bias".}}</ref>

A 2024 study found that [[large language models]] tend to provide more accurate information for major metropolitan areas than for smaller cities and regions. <ref>{{cite web |last1=Campanella |first1=Charlie |last2=van der Goot |first2=Rob |title=Big City Bias: Evaluating the Impact of Metropolitan Size on Computational Job Market Abilities of Language Models |url=https://aclanthology.org/2024.nlp4hr-1.6/ |publisher=Association for Computational Linguistics |date=March 2024 |access-date=September 25, 2025}}</ref>
